361.quote_or_event: “As the crane is produced from an egg, and the egg is produced from a crane, so they call desire the origin of delusion, and delusion the origin of desire. Love and hatred are caused by Karman, and they say that Karman has its origin in delusion; Karman is the root of birth and death, and birth and death they call misery.”
361.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana sets out a chain in which desire (Jacobi notes the original word is tṛṣṇā, craving) and delusion breed each other, delusion binds karmic matter to the soul, and that karma is the root of repeated birth and death.
361.tie_back: Valluvar calls desire the seed that unfailingly yields birth after birth for every being, and the Jain text traces the same line from craving through karma to the 'root of birth and death'.
361.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.6–7 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
361._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Close match: both make craving the generative cause of rebirth, though the Jain version runs it through delusion and karmic matter rather than using a seed image.

362.quote_or_event: “Sir, what does the soul obtain by the longing for liberation? By the longing for liberation the soul obtains an intense desire of the Law; by an intense desire of the Law he quickly arrives at an (increased) longing for liberation; he destroys anger, pride, deceit, and greed, which reproduce themselves infinitely.”
362.explanation: Saṃvega, the longing for liberation, is the first item in Mahāvīra's lecture on exertion in righteousness. It is the one desire Jainism encourages, because it feeds on itself and destroys the passions, greed included, that otherwise keep reproducing themselves.
362.tie_back: Valluvar says that if one must desire, one should desire freedom from birth, which comes through wanting to be free of wanting. Saṃvega is exactly that kind of redirected desire: a longing that wears away greed and leads toward the end of rebirth.
362.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 29.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
362._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit: the 'desire for liberation that destroys greed' matches the kural's paradox. The same paragraph goes on to say such a soul will not be born more than three more times, which echoes piravaamai, freedom from birth.

363.quote_or_event: “There is much happiness for the sage, for the houseless monk, who is free from all ties, and knows himself to be single and unconnected (with the rest of the world).” … “Here (on earth) you are the highest man, Reverend sir, and hereafter you will be the highest; exempt from all blemishes you will reach Perfection, a higher state than which there is none in this world.”
363.explanation: King Nami renounces Mithilā. When Indra, disguised as a Brāhmaṇa, urges him to fill his treasury with gold, silver and jewels, he refuses, saying that freedom from ties is true happiness. Indra then reveals himself and declares Nami the highest of men both here and hereafter.
363.tie_back: Valluvar calls freedom from desire a treasure without equal 'here' and 'there'. Nami turns down an actual treasury for that freedom and is praised as supreme in this world and the next.
363.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 9.16 and 9.58 (context 9.46–49) (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
363._accuracy_note: Both verses checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit, since the episode literally sets renounced wealth against the happiness of being free from ties, here and hereafter. It is a narrative illustration rather than a one-line maxim.

364.explanation: Among the ten supreme virtues (daśa-dharma) in Tattvārtha Sūtra 9.6, Pūjyapāda's classic commentary defines purity not as ritual cleanness but simply as the absence of greed. Supreme truthfulness (uttama satya) is listed as a companion virtue in the same sūtra.
364.tie_back: Valluvar defines purity as freedom from desire rather than as ritual washing. The Jain commentary gives almost the same definition, making śauca identical with freedom from lobha (greed).
364.source: Tattvārtha Sūtra 9.6, with Pūjyapāda's Sarvārthasiddhi (tr. Vijay K. Jain, 2018; wisdomlib.org)
364._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. Near one-to-one for the first line (purity = freedom from craving). The Jain text does not reproduce the kural's second line, that this freedom comes from longing for truth, beyond listing truthfulness as a sister virtue.

365.quote_or_event: “If an ordained monk, through carelessness, does not strictly keep the great vows, if he does not restrain himself, but desires pleasure, then his fetters will not be completely cut off.”
365.explanation: The ascetic in the Twentieth Lecture warns that taking orders is not enough. A monk who keeps the outward form but still desires pleasure remains bound, and the next verses call him 'empty like a clenched fist'.
365.tie_back: Valluvar says only those who have cut off desire are truly renunciants, and that others are not fully 'cut free'. The Jain verse says the same: a monk who still desires pleasure does not have his fetters completely cut off.
365.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 20.39 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
365._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Near one-to-one: both separate outward renunciation from inward freedom from desire, and both use the language of incomplete cutting. Jacobi notes that verses 38–53 may be a later addition to the lecture.

366.quote_or_event: “As the fruit of the Kimpâka is beautiful in taste and colour, when eaten; but destroys the life when digested, (being) poison; similar in their effect are pleasures.”
366.explanation: The kimpāka fruit, a recurring Jain image, tastes and looks sweet but is poison. Desire works the same way: it attracts at first and destroys afterwards, so the monk must stay on guard against it.
366.tie_back: Valluvar says that fearing desire is itself virtue because desire deceives and ruins a person. The kimpāka fruit is a picture of that deception, sweet on the tongue and deadly once swallowed.
366.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.20 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
366._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong thematic fit on desire as a deceiver. The kural's specific point that fearing desire is the virtue is implied by the verse, not stated in it.

367.quote_or_event: “He who endeavours to recognise the vanity of all desires, will arrive at perfect indifference. When he ceases to desire the objects (of the senses), his desire for pleasures will become extinct.” … “He will get rid of all misery which always afflicts mankind; recovered from the long illness, as it were, and glorious, he becomes infinitely happy, and obtains the (final) aim.”
367.explanation: The closing verses of the lecture on carelessness describe a sequence. Desire is fully extinguished, the obstructing karmas fall away, and the soul reaches its final aim, liberation, likened to recovery from a long illness.
367.tie_back: Valluvar promises that once desire is cut off completely, the deeds that lead to deathless life follow as one wishes. The Jain text likewise makes total extinction of desire the threshold beyond which the final aim is reached.
367.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.107 and 32.110 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
367._accuracy_note: Both verses checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit on 'total cutting of desire leads to liberation'. The kural's specific idea that the right deeds then come 'as one wishes' has no exact Jain counterpart.

368.quote_or_event: “Thus the objects of the senses and of the mind cause pain to passionate men, but they never in the least cause any pain to the dispassionate.”
368.explanation: After going through each of the senses in turn, the lecture concludes that suffering comes not from the objects themselves but from passionate attachment to them. The dispassionate meet the same objects and feel no pain.
368.tie_back: Valluvar says those without desire have no sorrow, while for those with desire sorrow comes without fail. The Jain verse states the same two-sided rule: pain for the passionate, none for the dispassionate.
368.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.100 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
368._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Near one-to-one in structure and claim. The kural's image of sorrow coming 'one after another' (menmel) is reflected elsewhere in the lecture (32.33, 'a long succession of pains') rather than in this verse.

369.quote_or_event: “From desire of pleasure arises the misery of the whole world, the gods included; whatever misery of body and mind there is, the dispassionate will put an end to it.”
369.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana treats desire for pleasure as the single source of all suffering, even that of the gods, and teaches that freedom from passion ends every bodily and mental misery.
369.tie_back: Valluvar calls desire the sorrow of sorrows, whose destruction brings unbroken joy even in this life. The Jain verse likewise makes desire the source of all the world's misery and dispassion its complete cure.
369.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.19 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
369._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit: desire as the root sorrow and dispassion as its end. The kural's stress on joy 'even here' (eendum) is only implicit in this verse.

370.quote_or_event: “The more you get, the more you want; your desires increase with your means. Though two mâshas would do to supply your want, still you would scarcely think ten millions sufficient.”
370.explanation: In the story Jacobi summarises from the commentary, the student Kapila is offered whatever he asks by a king. He keeps raising the sum in his mind until it reaches ten thousand millions. Then he suddenly sees that desire can never be filled, renounces on the spot as a self-enlightened sage, and speaks this verse.
370.tie_back: Valluvar says desire is by nature never satisfied, and whoever casts it off at once gains a nature that never changes. Kapila's verse states the insatiability, and his sudden enlightenment on giving desire up acts out the second line.
370.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 8.17, with Jacobi's note on the Kapila legend (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
370._accuracy_note: Verse checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The story is paraphrased from Jacobi's footnote, which relays the commentary. Near one-to-one on insatiable desire, and the legend supplies the 'immediate' transformation the kural describes.
